Hi Ben —

Thanks again for the demo last week. Our architecture team asked me to follow up with concrete questions: we need guidance on whether to connect our on-prem datacenter to Redwood Private via VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), or a site-to-site (S2S) VPN. Key constraints:

- We run two colocated data halls with mixed IPv4 ranges (some legacy overlaps possible).
- Expected steady-state egress: 400–800 Mbps, with occasional bursts to 1.5 Gbps.
- We need encrypted transit, predictable latency for inference calls (p95 < 100ms), and strict north-south access control.
- We also have a compliance requirement: we must restrict data plane egress to only whitelisted Redwood endpoints and have audit logs for connections.

Could you outline tradeoffs and a recommended path (including how transitive routing, IP overlap, MTU, and failover should be handled)? I attached a rough network diagram and our current IP allocations.

Appreciate any quick guidance — if helpful we can schedule a short call (30m).

Hi Javier — thanks for the diagram and constraints; good detail. High level recommendations up front, then specifics and a suggested fallback pattern.

High-level recommendation (short):
- Primary: PrivateLink (interface endpoints) to Redwood Private for control-plane and tokenized inference endpoints (best isolation, no cross-account route changes, avoids transitive routing issues).
- Secondary / backup: S2S VPN with BGP (IPSec) for failover and for maintenance/ingress that can tolerate higher variance in latency.
- VPC Peering: avoid as primary if you need cross-account transitive behavior or have overlapping IPs — peering does not support transitive routing and requires non-overlapping CIDRs. It’s useful inside an org or for very high-throughput low-latency private network between VPCs with non-overlapping ranges.

Why PrivateLink first:
- Security/isolation: traffic terminates at an ENI in the service VPC and is scoped to the service interface; you do not inject routes into your VPC route table that reach other provider VPCs. This aligns well with your compliance ask to whitelist endpoints and limit egress.
- No CIDR requirement: PrivateLink tolerates IP overlap because connections go over interface endpoints instead of peering routes.
- Simpler firewall rules: lock to endpoint ENI IPs and SGs.
- Operational: easier to rotate service backends and do model rollouts without changing your routing.

Limitations to watch for with PrivateLink:
- Bandwidth: single ENI throughput is limited by the instance/enclave; for 1+ Gbps you may need multiple interface endpoints or provisioned capacity on the Redwood side. We can provision multiple endpoint interfaces and do DNS/load-split.
- Latency: slightly higher than VPC peering for equivalent pathing, but usually well within p95 targets for inference if routed via a nearby region/connected colo. We can benchmark with a quick perf test.
- Costs: interface endpoints have per-hour and per-GB charges. We’ll share expected unit economics in the cheatsheet.

When VPC peering makes sense:
- When both sides control/allocation non-overlapping CIDRs and you need very high throughput with minimal added networking hops. If you plan to co-manage VPCs and want straight private L3 routing, peering is simple and low-latency.
- Drawbacks: no transitive routing (peering cannot route to other VPCs or transit gateway without additional constructs), and you must handle CIDR planning carefully.

When S2S VPN is appropriate:
- Quick to set up, encrypted IPSec path from on-prem to VPCs. Good for temporary/elevated-burst traffic or as a predictable backup.
- Less predictable latency/throughput than a dedicated private path; MTU and fragmentation can be issues (we recommend testing with your typical payload sizes and enabling MSS clamping as needed).

Operational pattern we recommend for EdgeBridge given your constraints:
1) Provision PrivateLink interface endpoints for Redwood inference endpoints in your VPC. Start with two endpoints in different AZs for redundancy.
2) Parallel: bring up an S2S VPN with BGP to the Redwood VPC as an active-passive failover (BGP MED or AS-path prepend to prefer PrivateLink in normal ops).
3) If sustained throughput needs exceed PrivateLink capacity, we’ll work with you to add additional endpoints or a dedicated direct connect/transit arrangement; we can also enable parallel TCP connections and connection pooling in the client SDK to spread load.
4) For overlapping IPs: use NAT at your edge for the subnets that conflict (we can document which prefixes to NAT) or put inference clients behind a NAT gateway specifically for calls to Redwood endpoints.
5) Audit & logging: we’ll provide endpoint IPs and certs; pair with your firewall rules to whitelist only those ENI IPs. We can also enable token-level request logging and provide audit exports for your compliance team.

Action items / asks from EdgeBridge:
- Confirm whether you can NAT conflicting prefixes (yes/no).
- Share an expected concurrent connection count and burst profile (peak tokens/sec).
- Confirm desirable maintenance window for failover testing.

I attached a short cheatsheet that summarizes the cost/throughput/latency tradeoffs and a sample MAP (mutual action plan) spreadsheet.

If helpful I’m free Tues 06/16 10–11am PT for a 30m call to walk through a proposed network change window. Kimberly and Sean are CC’d to help with procurement and operations checks.

Hi Javier — quick procurement / compliance notes to add to Ben’s excellent summary:

- Contracting: if you choose PrivateLink as primary, we’ll include the endpoint SKU in the Dedicated/Private addendum. That impacts billing cadence (monthly usage + endpoint hours).
- SLAs: PrivateLink endpoints can be part of our Dedicated capacity SLA; we’ll need to align region and AZ placement.
- Audit: we can provide network flow logs (flow logs + endpoint-level metrics) and a delivery window for SOC2 artifacts — please flag which artifacts you need (SOC2 Type II, data retention proof, encryption-at-rest attestation).
- Security: we recommend enabling mTLS between your clients and our SDK tokens where possible; we can provide guidance for cert pinning and short-lived tokens.

Operational ask: please share a primary contact for NetOps and the IP space you’re willing to NAT (if any). I’ll have procurement prepare a ballpark pricing estimate for PrivateLink + backup VPN by EOD Monday.

—Kimberly
Head of Customer Success Ops | Redwood Inference
